title: China cuts margin requirement to 80% in fresh market support push, but will it work?
body: The margin cut may help mainland sentiment at the open, especially in the high-beta growth names on ChiNext and the STAR board, where leveraged retail money tends to concentrate. Because the change only takes effect on 30 November, its direct flow impact is a week away, so traders may treat early gains as anticipatory and easy to reverse. Hong Kong-listed Chinese tech is outside the scope of the measures and stays more exposed to the global AI rout. The yuan is unlikely to react much unless the measures bring clear inflows back into mainland equities. ---- Earlier: Seoul readies a market fund unused since 2008 after the Kospi sinks --- Beijing is making it cheaper to borrow to buy stocks, but with margin balances already shrinking, the real shortage looks like confidence, not credit. Summary: China's three main exchanges will lower the minimum margin requirement for buying stocks on credit to 80% from 100%, effective 30 November, with CSRC approval. The move reverses a January tightening and applies to both new and existing contracts. Margin loans have fallen by more than 20% since late June, to about 2.2 trillion yuan. Chinese media estimate the change could free up close to 400 billion yuan. The Shanghai and Shenzhen exchanges and the national clearing house announced fee cuts, and Shenzhen proposed market makers for ChiNext. The steps follow a broader 2 November support package after mainland stocks' worst month in a decade.

title: Australia flash PMI sinks to 46.1 as private sector shrinks at fastest pace in 5 years
body: A drop this deep, alongside the first easing in input cost inflation for months, weakens the case for further Australian monetary tightening. That leaves the Australian dollar exposed if rate markets start pricing a gentler path. The sharp fall in new export orders also points to softening external demand, at a time when global equities are already under heavy pressure. Prices are still running above their long-run averages, though, so policymakers are unlikely to move quickly to declare inflation beaten. Traders may also treat the flash reading cautiously until the final data in early December. --- Higher interest rates are now hitting Australian demand across the board: services have joined manufacturing in contraction, new orders are at a five-year low and confidence is draining away. Summary: Australia's flash composite PMI fell to 46.1 in November from 48.2, the lowest since August 2021 and a second month in contraction. Services activity slid to 46.2 from 48.5, and the manufacturing PMI eased to 48.7 from 49.6. New orders fell at the fastest pace since August 2021, with services new business falling faster than manufacturing. Export orders fell at the sharpest rate in just over two years. Firms cut staff and cleared backlogs, and business confidence hit a three-year low. Input cost and selling price inflation both eased but remain above their long-run averages. Final data are due on 1 December for manufacturing and 3 December for services and the composite.

title: Goldman names 3 signals that could mark a bottom as the S&P 500 sits 12% below its record
body: Goldman's positioning data suggests that last week's rout cleared out mainly the fast money. Mutual funds, ETF buyers and asset managers are still heavily long, which leaves room for more forced or discretionary selling before any bottom forms. A December hike is close to fully priced and no Fed pivot is in sight, so AI earnings news is the most likely of the three catalysts to change the picture. The shift toward a growth downgrade favours defensive sectors and government bonds over cyclicals. It could also weigh on demand-sensitive commodities if it persists. --- Hedge funds have already run for the exits, but Goldman's data shows the rest of the market is still long and waiting for a reason to stop selling. Summary: Goldman Sachs names three possible triggers for a bottom in the US equity correction: more confidence in AI-linked earnings, a dovish Fed signal, or a sharp further drop in investor positioning. The S&P 500 is about 12% below its 6 October record and the Nasdaq 100 about 20%. Goldman's AI basket is down roughly 32%. Hedge fund net leverage is at its lowest since April 2025, but Goldman's broader sentiment indicator, at 0.7, is still above average. Equity funds have taken in nearly $170 billion since the start of the fourth quarter, and asset managers' futures positioning is in the 82nd percentile. Goldman targets 8,700 on the S&P 500 by end-2027, with a newer scenario range of about 5,800 to 8,100.

title: Australia's Services Sector Contraction Deepens as S&P Global PMI Falls to 46.2 in November
body: Australia's services sector slipped further into contraction in November, with the S&P Global Services PMI declining to 46.2, down from 48.5 in October 2026. The latest reading, updated on 22 November 2026, underscores mounting pressures on the country's largest economic sector. The drop from October's already sub-50 level signals that business activity in services is weakening at a faster pace, with the index remaining below the 50-point threshold that typically separates expansion from contraction. The deterioration between October and November suggests that demand conditions and overall sentiment in the services economy may be softening further as the year draws to a close. With two consecutive months of readings under 50, the data point to a sustained downturn in Australian services activity through the fourth quarter of 2026, raising concerns about broader implications for growth and employment in the sector. Policymakers and market participants are likely to watch upcoming releases closely for signs of stabilization or further weakness. title: Australia's Factory Activity Slips Deeper into Contraction in November, S&P Global PMI Falls to 48.7
body: Australia's manufacturing sector weakened further in November, with the S&P Global Manufacturing PMI edging down to 48.7 from 49.6 in October 2026, according to data updated on 22 November 2026. The reading remains below the 50.0 threshold that separates expansion from contraction, indicating a deepening slowdown in factory activity. The November decline suggests that underlying pressures facing Australian manufacturers—such as softer demand conditions and cautious business sentiment—continued to weigh on output and new orders through the month. While the drop from October is modest, the move further below 50.0 underscores a more entrenched contractionary phase for the sector as the year draws to a close. Investors and policymakers are likely to watch upcoming data closely for signs of stabilization. A sustained period below the 50.0 mark could reinforce expectations of a more subdued industrial backdrop heading into 2027 and may factor into assessments of monetary and fiscal policy support for the broader economy. title: Australia's Private Sector Slump Deepens as November S&P Global PMI Falls to 46.1
body: Australia's private sector downturn intensified in November, with the S&P Global Manufacturing & Services PMI slipping further into contraction territory. The composite indicator declined to 46.10 in November 2026, down from 48.20 in October 2026, on a month-over-month basis. The latest reading, updated on 22 November 2026, signals a sharper deterioration in business conditions across both manufacturing and services. With the PMI remaining below the 50-point threshold and moving lower compared with the previous month, the data point to weakening activity and rising headwinds for Australia's economy as the year draws to a close. The comparison shows that while October had already marked a contraction versus the prior month, November's print underscores an acceleration in the downturn, highlighting mounting pressure on output and demand across the private sector. Investors and policymakers will be closely watching upcoming data for signs of stabilization or further weakening. The material has been provided by InstaForex Company - www.instaforex.com

title: New Zealand Q3 Retail Sales Rebound 2.2% QoQ, Snapping Previous Quarter's Decline
body: New Zealand's retail sector staged a solid recovery in the third quarter of 2026, with sales rising 2.2% quarter-over-quarter, according to data updated on 22 November 2026. The rebound follows a 0.4% quarter-on-quarter decline in the second quarter of 2026, marking a clear turnaround in consumer spending momentum. On a quarter-over-quarter comparison basis, the latest figure shows that retailers moved from contraction to meaningful growth within a single quarter. The "actual" measure reflects the change from the second to the third quarter of 2026, while the "previous" figure captured the decline from the first to the second quarter of 2026. This shift suggests improving demand conditions and may ease some concerns about a prolonged soft patch in household consumption. While the underlying drivers of the rebound were not detailed in the release, the sharp swing from -0.4% to 2.2% is likely to draw close attention from businesses and policymakers, as stronger retail activity can signal firmer overall economic growth heading into the end of 2026. title: New Zealand Retail Sales Edge Higher in Q3 2026, Signalling Steady Consumer Demand
body: New Zealand's retail sector recorded a modest acceleration in annual growth in the third quarter of 2026, underscoring resilient consumer demand despite a challenging global backdrop. Retail sales rose 3.5% compared with the same period a year earlier, slightly above the 3.3% year‑on‑year increase registered in the second quarter of 2026. The latest data, updated on 22 November 2026, indicate that consumer spending is continuing to expand at a measured pace, with the incremental uptick suggesting that households are still willing to spend, though without a sharp surge in momentum. The improvement from the previous quarter's reading points to a retail environment that remains supportive of overall economic activity as the year progresses. With two consecutive quarters of low‑to‑mid single‑digit growth, the figures suggest a pattern of steady rather than spectacular expansion in New Zealand's retail landscape, a dynamic closely watched by market participants assessing the health of domestic demand and its implications for the wider economy. title: California widens Nvidia probe to criminal law, a bigger deal than Huang return talk
body: An open-ended state criminal investigation, on top of an SEC probe, adds a legal risk premium that's hard to price. That could cap Nvidia rebounds even as the broader market steadies. The stock's weight in major indices means headline risk here can spill into the Nasdaq and the wider AI trade, and into Asian chip names already under pressure. Investors may also start pricing a lower chance of Huang returning, which removes one potential upside catalyst that some had been counting on. The board's subpoena response and any disclosure in regulatory filings are the near-term flashpoints. Newswire cut: California's Nvidia probe now covers possible criminal breaches of state law over China chip sales and whether Nvidia or ex-CEO Jensen Huang misled the public, AG Rob Bonta said. The SEC is also investigating, raising the stakes for any Huang return. One-line wrap: The market has been arguing about whether Huang comes back, while California has been quietly building a case that could make that question irrelevant. Summary: California AG Rob Bonta says his Nvidia investigation covers potential criminal violations of state law. The probe examines whether Nvidia or Huang gave false information about chip sales to China, and whether investors were misled. It is preliminary, with no conclusions. Bonta served Nvidia with an investigative subpoena on 19 November, a week after Huang resigned. The SEC is also investigating, reportedly including whether Nvidia misled investors.

title: OCBC: AI rout becomes a growth shock as EM currencies take the dollar's strength
body: If OCBC is right, dollar strength will be most visible in high-yielding and externally exposed EM currencies. That makes the case for selective EM FX hedges even while the dollar softens against the majors. Carry trades funded in low-yielders are vulnerable to further unwinding if the AI sell-off resumes, which could add volatility to Asian currencies, especially those tied to chip exports. A clearer Fed pause signal, along the lines JPMorgan's Kelly expects, would be the main thing that could ease the pressure on EM. Any repeat of last week's forced selling in metals would support the "growth shock" reading. - The AI unwind has stopped being just a rates story, OCBC says, and emerging market currencies are paying for the dollar's resilience. Summary: OCBC strategists say the interest rate shock may have evolved into a growth shock, as AI de-risking hits equities, EM carry trades and metals. Concerns over the AI investment cycle have lowered stocks and US yields, shifting the pressure from the stronger dollar onto EM currencies. They expect the dollar to stay supported in the short term by hawkish Fed risk and tightening global financial conditions. In October, OCBC's Sim Moh Siong and Christopher Wong warned that a US-centric AI shock could hurt the dollar. By November they expected it to stay firm into 1H27. The "growth shock" framing echoes Goldman Sachs' view that the sell-off has broadened beyond an AI unwind.

title: JPMorgan's Kelly: tech correction overdue, stocks to bounce, Fed to hike once then pause
body: Kelly's one-hike-then-pause view gives bulls a counter-narrative to the hawkish pricing that has weighed on stocks and gold. If December's statement or projections lean his way, front-end yields and the dollar could ease. Waller's push for 50bp, or a clear signal of a January follow-up, remains the main risk to that view. November CPI is now a key data point: a sizeable gasoline-driven drop would strengthen the case for a pause. Kelly's flow argument (401(k)s, buybacks, wealthy buyers) suggests dips may keep attracting support, even if the AI valuation debate isn't settled. --- Earlier: US stock futures jump over 2% in relief bounce, gold rallies, but Kospi slides nearly 4% --- Kelly sees a healthy tech shakeout, a cooling economy outside AI and a Fed that hikes once and stops, a much gentler script than the one markets traded last week. Summary: JPMorgan Asset Management's David Kelly says a tech correction was overdue, driven by Nvidia's problems and wider disruption. He sees little strong demand outside tech and expects falling gasoline prices to cut about 0.4 points from November's annual CPI rate. He expects a December Fed hike followed by a pause, and says Waller is largely alone in backing 50bp. Waller has said the Fed should hike 50bp in December or signal a January follow-up. Dallas Fed President Logan has also shown openness to faster tightening. Kelly expects steady inflows from 401(k)s, buybacks and wealthy investors to help the market bounce.

title: Ackman urges Fed to drop 2% inflation goal for 3%, warns 9 December hike risks recession
body: Ackman's post adds to a growing chorus, now including the Treasury, arguing against further Fed hikes. That could feed hopes of a softer message on 9 December even if the hike itself goes ahead. Rate markets are unlikely to shift much on investor commentary alone. Any sign that Fed officials are open to slowing the pace, though, would weigh on the dollar and front-end yields and support equities and gold. His SpaceX example also points to strain in credit markets, so corporate bond spreads are worth watching as a gauge of how much tightening is already in the system. --- Earlier: Could Nvidia shareholders force Huang back? The 15% hurdle behind a long-shot idea --- Ackman wants the Fed to move the goalposts to 3%, but a central bank that changes its target mid-fight risks losing the credibility it needs to win it. Summary: Pershing Square CEO Bill Ackman says the Fed is set to make a mistake at its 9 December meeting. He says financial conditions have tightened massively, citing SpaceX's secured debt at around 8.3% against below 6% for its IPO-era unsecured bonds, plus a higher cost of equity after the sell-off. He argues 2% is unrealistic given geopolitics, defence spending, deglobalisation, tariffs and AI-related investment, and that 3% is more realistic. He warns that more hikes aimed at reaching 2% would push the US and the world into recession.

title: US stock futures jump over 2% in relief bounce, gold rallies, but Kospi slides nearly 4%
body: The bounce looks driven by positioning and policy headlines, not by any change in the AI valuation debate. Rallies could fade quickly if cash markets in New York don't confirm the futures move. Gold rising alongside stocks suggests margin-call selling has paused, which makes the metal a useful real-time gauge of whether deleveraging pressure is returning. Higher US yields and a firmer USD/JPY show some haven demand unwinding, with the yen on the soft side in holiday-thinned trade. The Shanghai and Hong Kong open is the next test, given Beijing's new margin rules and the brokerages' talk of a bottom. --- Wall Street's futures have found their feet after a brutal last week, but with Seoul still sliding and Tokyo away, this is a breather until proven otherwise. Summary: S&P 500 futures rose about 2.2% and Nasdaq 100 futures about 2.8% in early Asian trade, near session highs. Spot gold rallied about 2.3% to around $3,620, and silver rose around 2.6%. Brent slipped to near $90 and WTI to around $83. The dollar eased against most majors, with AUD/USD up about 0.4%, but USD/JPY rose to near 158.90. The Kospi fell nearly 4% to around 4,680, with Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix sharply lower. Japan was closed, and China and Hong Kong had yet to open. The US 10-year yield rose to about 4.95%.

title: Goldman sees European gas halving to €45 in 2027, but a cold winter could push it to €150
body: A credible path to much cheaper gas would ease pressure on Europe's energy-intensive industries and utilities' input costs, and could weigh on gas futures further out the curve even while the winter contracts stay volatile. For oil, Goldman's surplus view gives bears a medium-term anchor. The near-term risks still point higher, though, while Gulf disruption continues, so dips may be shallow until flows clearly normalise. Lower energy import bills would remove one of the structural headwinds that has weighed on the euro. Rate differentials with a hiking Fed are likely to stay the dominant FX driver for now. --- Last week: Goldman sees Brent at $78 by end-2027 as oil surplus returns, flags near-term upside risk Goldman Sachs gets bearish on oil prices but doesn't see help for consumers --- Goldman sees Europe's gas bill roughly halving next year, but the forecast has to get through a winter first. Summary: Goldman Sachs forecasts European LNG prices averaging around €45/MWh in 2027, down from about €85 in mid-November. Its equity team sees TTF at around €31 by end-2027. In oil, the bank sees Brent averaging $88 in 2027 and easing to $78 by December, as a surplus of about 2 million bpd builds. Gulf exporters are adapting through new bypass pipelines, ship-to-ship transfers and naval escorts. LNG has adapted less well because it's harder to move. In a cold winter with Gulf LNG exports at 25% to 30% of pre-war levels, gas could near €150 in the first quarter.

title: Chinese brokers see a bottom and a broader 2027 rally after Beijing's support push
body: The brokers' calls point to two phases. Near term, rotation favours high-dividend defensives such as banks, insurers, utilities-style infrastructure and consumer staples like baijiu. In any rebound, beta should lead, through ChiNext growth names, small caps and technology. The combination of official support measures and upbeat state-linked research may limit downside in large caps in the near term. Without a pickup in leveraged and foreign inflows, though, rallies may struggle to stick. Moves in margin balances after 30 November and northbound flows will be the gauges to watch. --- Beijing announced the support, and China's big brokers are now explaining how to trade it, which is familiar choreography in a market where policy and research tend to move together. Summary: CITIC Securities says the 22 November package targets the market's main pressures and signals a commitment to stability. It sees valuation opportunities in quality leaders and expects a broader rally next year, favouring diversified exposure focused on sector leaders. China Securities says high-dividend defensives still offer strong value while the market bottoms. It favours banks, white goods, baijiu, home textiles, insurers, railways and highways, telecoms, and shipping and ports. It warns that dividend stocks could lag in a rebound, while small caps, tech, growth and thematic plays outperform.

title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6775 – Reuters estimate
body: The People's Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. --- Earlier: China cuts margin requirement to 80% in fresh market support push, but will it work? --- China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks.

title: The AI winners may not exist yet, J.P. Morgan warns, as mega-IPOs flood the market
body: J.P. Morgan's numbers push back on one popular explanation for the AI sell-off, that a flood of new shares is draining liquidity. That puts the focus back on valuations and earnings doubts as the real drivers. Strong household, foreign and buyback demand also suggests a deep pool of buyers if sentiment stabilises, which supports the buy-the-dip case. The point that much of the value creation now happens before listing is a caution for anyone chasing new AI listings, and it could weigh on post-IPO performance. --- Earlier: Goldman names 3 signals that could mark a bottom as the S&P 500 sits 12% below its record --- The AI listing boom is huge in dollar terms but small next to the market absorbing it, and J.P. Morgan suggests the next big winners may still be private, or not yet born. Summary: J.P. Morgan Private Bank expects US IPO proceeds of around $290 billion in 2026, close to the 2021 peak of about $330 billion. That is less than 1% of a roughly $70 trillion US stock market. SpaceX and Anthropic alone have raised more than $179 billion this year. Demand is growing faster than supply: households bought more than $800 billion of equities in the first half, foreign investors over $350 billion, and buybacks have topped $1.3 trillion. An estimated 85% to 95% of companies with more than $100 million in revenue remain private, and unicorns are worth about $8 trillion. The bank warned that the eventual AI winners may not exist yet.

title: SNB's Martin eyes second-round effects after inflation jumps to 1.5%, hike in view
body: Martin's focus on second-round effects is a hawkish signal, and it supports pricing for a December SNB hike. A tightening Swiss central bank alongside a hiking Fed changes the usual rate-differential story for the franc. Combined with strong safe-haven demand during the equity rout, that could keep the franc well bid, especially against the euro. That is the very currency risk Martin flagged, so the SNB may stay willing to lean against excessive franc strength even as it tightens. UBS shares remain exposed to headlines on the capital rules and any further talk of a headquarters move. --- Swiss inflation is still within target, but its speed has the SNB watching wages and prices closely, and a December hike now looks like a live option. Summary: SNB Vice Chairman Antoine Martin told Le Matin Dimanche the bank is paying particular attention to possible second-round inflation effects. Swiss annual inflation rose faster than expected to 1.5% in October from 1% in September, raising expectations of a December hike. The SNB targets 0% to 2%. Chairman Martin Schlegel had said the jump surprised the bank. Martin said the franc "very clearly" remains a safe haven and named exchange-rate swings as the SNB's main risk. He reiterated SNB support for requiring UBS to fully capitalise its foreign subsidiaries and said any headquarters move would be for UBS management to decide.

title: Gold sinks 9% in a week as margin calls and Fed hike bets override its haven role
body: Gold is currently trading as a funding asset, so its near-term direction depends more on equity volatility and leveraged positioning than on traditional safe-haven demand. A December Fed hike is close to fully priced, so further downside from rates alone may be limited. The bigger risk is another wave of liquidation if the AI sell-off deepens. Spot is now far below every major bank's year-end target, so forecast cuts could keep coming, which may weigh on sentiment even if outright selling slows. A sustained halt in equity losses is likely to be the first trigger for bargain hunting. --- Last week: Gold at $3,625: five forces behind the sell-off, and four reasons buyers haven't quit --- In this sell-off, gold isn't the shelter. It's one of the first things investors sell to cover losses elsewhere. Summary: Spot gold fell about 2.7% on Friday to around $3,525 an ounce, a 14-month low, and lost roughly 9% over the week, its worst week in eight months. The metal is now more than a third below its January record above $5,500. ING's Ewa Manthey cited higher rate expectations and a firmer dollar, and said the equity rout may have prompted selling to raise cash. Commerzbank's Carsten Fritsch pointed to renewed forced selling. Goldman Sachs, after two forecast cuts this month, sees gold at $4,150 by end-2026 and $4,650 by end-2027. Gold has lost its role as a refuge in the current market rout.

title: Korea's market rescue fund is worth around $8 billion, but is 10.76 trillion won enough?
body: The fund's size makes it more of a confidence signal than a market mover, so traders are likely to watch how quickly and how visibly it is deployed, not just its headline value. If it is activated and the selling doesn't slow, pressure could build for a larger fund or for the outright short-selling curbs that authorities have so far avoided. Heavy foreign short positioning also leaves room for sharp short-covering rallies if sentiment turns, which could make Kospi swings even wider in both directions this week. Any further weakness in Korean equities may also feed through to the won via foreign outflows. --- Earlier: Seoul readies a market fund unused since 2008 after the Kospi sinks China cuts margin requirement to 80% in fresh market support push, but will it work? --- Korea has dusted off an $8 billion backstop for a market that can trade several times that in a single day, so its real value may be the signal it sends. Summary: Korea's stock market stabilisation fund is worth 10.76 trillion won, around $8 billion, SBS reported. It is financed by financial institutions. That matches the fund set up in 2020. If deployed, it would be the first use since 2008. The package also eases buyback limits and launches a three-month crackdown on illegal short selling, but stops short of a short-selling ban. Foreign investors made up nearly 80% of the roughly 5 trillion won of short-selling volume last week.

title: Could Nvidia shareholders force Huang back? The 15% hurdle behind a long-shot idea
body: For now this is a watch item, not a trading catalyst. There's no filing, no coalition and a board that has firmly closed the door. If it did escalate into a formal fight, the leadership uncertainty would likely weigh on Nvidia shares in the near term, whatever the outcome, at a time when AI stocks are already under heavy pressure. Some investors would treat a credible path back for Huang as positive for strategic continuity, which is why any SEC filings showing coordinated holders would draw immediate attention. The export compliance review is still the more important driver for the stock. --- A shareholder revolt to bring Huang back makes a good headline, but with no filing, a 15% threshold and a board that has said no, it's one to watch, not one to bet on. Summary: Activist investor Bill Ackman says Huang's backers could seek a special shareholder meeting and that the threat of a vote might sway the board. He doesn't plan to get involved. No formal campaign, filing or special meeting request has been reported. Nvidia's bylaws require holders with 15% of voting power, held for a year, to call a special meeting. Huang owns about 3.6%. Board chair Harvey Jones and interim CEO Colette Kress say the board won't reinstate Huang. Pressure is coming from an open letter, some investors, President Trump and, as of Sunday, a softer stance from Treasury Secretary Bessent.

title: Bessent leaves door open to Huang return at Nvidia, a week after urging an outside CEO
body: Removing Washington's apparent veto on Huang lowers one source of leadership uncertainty at the world's most important AI chipmaker, which could ease some of the pressure on Nvidia after last week's slide. The bigger regulatory overhang is still there, though. Any finding of export-control breaches could bring penalties or tighter limits on China-linked sales, which would hit revenue expectations directly. Traders are likely to treat the board's compliance response as a binary event for the stock and for AI sentiment more broadly. A clean answer would also strengthen the case for a Huang return. --- Earlier: US equity rout: Bessent cautions Fed against overtightening, before its December decision --- A week ago Bessent wanted an outsider running Nvidia. Now the door is open for Huang, as long as the compliance answers hold up. Summary: On CBS on Sunday, Bessent declined to rule out Jensen Huang returning as Nvidia CEO, saying it depends on "where the buck stops." On Fox News on 15 November, he had called for a shake-up and an outside successor, and gave Nvidia 10 days to answer compliance questions. He said he assumed Huang didn't know a woman linked to the scandal was an alleged spy, and said his "culture of non-compliance" remark described a possibility.
